top_story: Renewed fighting in Yemen has moved beyond a military contest into a systemic social collapse, pushing children out of school and into labor by 28 September and, a day later, driving a health system already battered by years of war toward breaking point as cholera and other diseases spread. These back-to-back indicators show a conflict now degrading family survival, education, and public health in tandem, which sharply raises the risk of longer-term social damage even if front lines stabilize. In Gaza, the postwar landscape remains defined by 61 million tonnes of rubble that may conceal up to 10,000 bodies and unexploded ordnance, turning recovery into a slow, hazardous process that prolongs trauma and blocks basic reconstruction. The regional picture is one of wars that continue to kill indirectly after peak combat, as collapsed services, displacement, and wrecked urban space deepen civilian harm and delay any meaningful recovery.
